- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	# Where the language rules came from
2	
3	This document is the record behind the rules this project states about its own writing. It answers one
4	question: why does a given rule say what it says. It covers the readings that produced the rules, and
5	the procedure that turns a repeated reader stop into a rule.
6	
7	live-spec is this project: a set of skills, scripts, and gates that a person and an agent use together
8	to write, prove, and ship software. A gate is a script that refuses a commit or a push when the thing
9	it guards is wrong. The texts described below are this project's own documents.
10	
11	Three pages carry these rules, and each has one reader.
12	
13	- `docs/language-rules.md` is the writer's page. It states every rule in the words a writer applies to
14	  a sentence, and it defines the six surfaces with an example of each.
15	- `docs/language-rule-coverage.md` is the maintainer's page. It carries what catches a break of each
16	  rule, how far that catcher reaches, where it is armed, and how to run each kind of catcher by hand.
17	- This page is the record. Read it to know why a rule exists.
18	
19	Each rule carries a short identifier such as `r02`, and this page names a rule by that identifier
20	together with the rule's short name in italics, a clause naming the defect the rule removes. An
21	identifier is never reused: a retired rule takes its identifier out of the set, and no later rule takes
22	it back.
23	
24	<!-- generated:rule-home-totals — scripts/gen-language-consumers.py owns the block below -->
25	
26	The rule home carries 66 rules and its highest identifier is `r75`, so nine stand retired.
27	
28	<!-- /generated:rule-home-totals -->
29	
30	Of those, seven went in the fold recorded below, `r22` was folded into `r01` earlier, and `r28` left
31	with no record of why.
32	
33	<!-- generated:vocabulary — scripts/gen-language-consumers.py owns the block below -->
34	
35	## The words on this page
36	
37	The words these rules are stated in. Every page built from this home carries this block, so a reader holding one page holds every word that page uses. A word is defined here when two or more pages need it; a word one page alone needs is defined on that page.
38	
39	- **class** — the shape of a mistake: the form it takes wherever it turns up.
40	- **break** — one place a text falls short of a rule, being a single instance of the class that rule names.
41	- **catcher** — whatever finds a break: a literal pattern in a script, a model reading for meaning, or a person reading the text.
42	- **home** — the one file a given fact is written in.
43	- **the rule home** — the file `guardrails/language-rules.json`, where every rule is edited and nowhere else, and from which every page here is built.
44	- **rule** — one statement about one class, written as one entry in the rule home.
45	- **surface** — a kind of text rather than a file, so one file carries several; this project names six, and each rule binds the ones it applies to.
46	- **stop** — one place a reader could not go on, had to read twice, or had to guess.
47	- **a blocking stop** — a stop where the reader could not go on with the text, or would have acted on the text wrongly; every other stop is one the reader noticed and read past.
48	- **register** — the rules a surface's text is held to: which words, which sentence shapes, and how it addresses its reader.
49	
50	Five roles appear wherever these rules are discussed.
51	
52	- **the writer** — whoever drafts a text: a person, or the agent working for one.
53	- **the reader** — whoever reads that text afterwards, carrying whatever context they happen to have.
54	- **a cold reader** — a reader given the text alone, with no repository, no earlier drafts, and no way to ask the writer a question.
55	- **the maintainer** — whoever builds the catchers and repairs them.
56	- **the owner** — the one person whose project this is.
57	
58	One person often holds more than one of these roles in a day.
59	
60	<!-- /generated:vocabulary -->
61	
62	Three words on this page name three different things, and one of them was long written as one word for
63	all three. The **rule home** is the file every rule is edited in. **Where a wording was learned** is the
64	skill file, template, or habit a defect came out of, and this page says that in full each time. The
65	`sources` field on a rule entry is neither: it lists the files that stated that rule in prose before the
66	rule home existed, and the maintainer's page prints it.
67	
68	## How a cold reading is run
69	
70	Every cold reading recorded below was made by a model in a fresh session with none of this project
71	loaded. The procedure stands in `skills/text-audit/SKILL.md`, and the prompt handed to the reader
72	stands beside it in `skills/text-audit/references/reader-prompt.md`; a reading comes back as a file
73	under `docs/language-reads/`, named for its date and its number.
74	
75	A single stop is written down and opens nothing. A rule enters this project when the place that produced
76	that stop produces it again, the second occurrence proving the wording's origin rather than the one
77	sentence. Some rules came from a cold reader stopping and some from the owner; the readings below name
78	which produced what.
79	
80	## The one obligation
81	
82	The writer owes the reader every word, number, and list the writing depends on. That debt is measured on
83	a cold reader, who brings nothing to the text. Each of those words, numbers, and lists therefore stands
84	where it is used, or in one named place the sentence points to. A text that holds for a cold reader
85	holds for every other reader, whatever context that reader arrived with.
86	
87	Every rule on the writer's page names one way a text falls short of that obligation.
88	
89	## The readings that produced the rules
90	
91	The last section below holds this page's own readings, which are still going on.
92	
93	### Two cold readers, 2026-07-27
94	
95	The English reader was given six requirements from the spec (`PRODUCT_SPEC.md`) with its glossary held
96	back. The text used ten ordinary English nouns for jobs only this project knows, and used "red" as a
97	verb meaning to report something as a failure. Four of the ten — home, seat, law, and tier — turn up
98	again on this page. All of them stand here as instances of the class this reader met, and not as a
99	vocabulary to carry onward. That finding opened no rule of its own. The class was already in the rule
100	home as `r01`, *an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning*, whose entry names the skill and
101	profile files that stated it in prose before the rule home existed, so this reading stands as evidence
102	for that rule rather than its origin.
103	
104	Of the six requirements, that reader could implement two from the text alone. For a third the reader
105	wrote down the questions the requirement left unanswered and left it unimplemented, a cold reading
106	having no channel to ask them. The remaining three went unattempted: they depend on lists and on default
107	values the text gave nowhere.
108	
109	The Russian reader was given six paragraphs of working chat, about 250 words meant to be read straight
110	through, and stopped twenty times. Working chat is what a person and an agent write to each other while
111	the work is going on. Every word that stopped that reader was made by translating an English term of
112	this project's own into Russian, one word at a time. The result each time was a real Russian word that
113	carries none of the meaning this project gives it. The writer's page records those words with their
114	plain replacements, under `r02`, *a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain
115	standard word exists*.
116	
117	That reader also named two habits without being asked, and both are rules today. Actions handed to
118	things that cannot perform them are `r05`, *a predicate applied to a subject that cannot carry it*. One
119	thing carrying two names in neighbouring sentences is `r04`, *one thing answering to a second name*.
120	
121	### The owner's reading of a rewrite, 2026-07-27
122	
123	Later the same day the owner read a first rewrite, drafted in chat and applying these rules, and
124	stopped at six of its sentences. Two of the six were the rewrite breaking a rule in the same passage
125	that stated it, and this page carries those two.
126	
127	- One sentence stated the rule that a criterion carries one trigger and one response, and broke two
128	  rules while stating it. «Триггер» is the English word trigger respelled in Russian letters, where
129	  Russian already has a plain word for it, which is `r02`. «Обязанность» is a plain Russian word
130	  standing in the wrong slot: it means an obligation, and it stood where the response belonged, which
131	  is the one-trigger-one-response rule the sentence had just stated.
132	- Another sentence banned coined names while coining one: «хвост без глагола», a tail with no verb. The
133	  thing that phrase points at is real, and it already had a plain name — a phrase with no finite verb.
134	  The writer's page carries it under that plain name, as `r36`, *a criterion closing on a phrase with
135	  no finite verb*. The coined phrase went, and the class it pointed at stayed.
136	
137	A sentence that states a rule is the first test of that rule, and it is the sentence to check first in
138	anything written here.
139	
140	### A cold reader given the rules page and a real job, 2026-07-28
141	
142	On 2026-07-28 a cold reader was handed `docs/language-rules.md` as it then stood, one page carrying
143	every rule and every catcher together, with a job to judge it against: write one page of documentation
144	tomorrow and hold it to this rulebook. That reading is recorded at
145	`docs/language-reads/2026-07-28-read1-language-rules-reference.md`.
146	
147	That reader could apply thirty of the sixty rules the rule home then carried to tomorrow's page. Eight
148	of the thirty need no judgment at all, because each ships a word list or a fixed shape; the reading
149	names those eight by identifier, and the other twenty-two turn on the reader's own judgment. All thirty
150	assume an answer to which surface a documentation page is: it is human-prose, and it carries the
151	artifact surface as well once it is published outside the project. Without that answer a writer is left
152	with the four rules that bind every surface: `r10`, *a thing named by denying its neighbour*; `r12`, *a
153	word grading how important or how good a thing is*; `r18`, *the language each surface is written in*,
154	which puts documents and published pages in English and conversation in the owner's own language; and
155	`r61`, *a defect recorded as examples with no class behind them*. The surfaces were the axis the whole
156	page was organized on, and the page defined none of them. The writer's page carries all six today,
157	placing a documentation page among them, written later that same day in answer to this reading.
158	
159	Three findings changed the shape of the rules rather than the wording of one entry.
160	
161	- The reader passed over four things carried in every entry and reported that none of them changes a
162	  word a writer writes: the files that stated the rule in prose before the rule home existed; two
163	  pieces of what catches a break, being how far each catcher reaches and the text the judging model is
164	  handed; and the half of the notes carrying what the entry was folded out of. All four are the
165	  maintainer's material, all four now stand on the maintainer's page, and the writer's page carries what
166	  a writer applies.
167	- Six rules named a list and gave it nowhere. A script catcher keeps the words it matches in a
168	  configuration file of its own, beside the script, as `guardrails/weak-words.json` stands beside
169	  `guardrails/check-weak-words.py`. Every one of those six lists now stands inside the rule that names
170	  it, read out of such a file at the moment the page is built. Three of the six had no such file: their
171	  words sat inside a script's regular expressions, where one edit reached the script and no edit reached
172	  the page. Those three lists moved into a configuration file beside their script, and the script now
173	  reads its own list from that file, so one edit reaches both.
174	- Five classes stood spread across twelve entries. The twelve are folded back into five, and each
175	  survivor's notes name the identifiers retired.
176	
177	### The readings of this page, 2026-07-27 to 2026-07-28
178	
179	This page has been given to a cold reader thirteen times and has failed every time. The bar is two
180	readings in a row returning nothing blocking, and that bar is itself one of the rules (`r54`, *a changed
181	section shipped before two clean cold readings*). Until it is cleared this page is shown to nobody, with
182	one exception: a reading is how the bar gets measured, so the reader running one is handed the page
183	while the bar is still unmet.
184	
185	- Readings one through four left no file of their own. `JOURNAL.md`, this project's dated log of what
186	  changed and why, carries them in a single sentence: that the page failed four readings and took five
187	  repair rounds. It gives no stop count and no finding from any of the four.
188	- Readings five through thirteen each left a file under `docs/language-reads/` named for its date and
189	  its number, the fifth being `2026-07-27-read5-language-defects.md`. The fifth ran on 2026-07-27 and
190	  the rest on 2026-07-28. In order they returned 45 stops with 11 blocking, then 34 with 8, 27 with 12,
191	  28 with 6, 31 with 5, 25 with 5, 25 with 6, 25 with 5, and 28 with 8.
192	
193	The blocking count over those nine readings ran 11, 8, 12, 6, 5, 5, 6, 5, 8, and never approached zero.
194	Two things kept it there, and both are visible in the readings themselves.
195	
196	The seventh reading returned fewer stops than the sixth, at 27 against 34, and more blocking ones, at 12
197	against 8. Between those two readings this page had taken on instructions for running the catchers, and
198	four of the seventh reading's twelve blocking stops sat on that new material: two on one script given as
199	an example of a script catcher and called the model catcher twenty-five lines later, one on a section
200	headed for running the person catcher that carried no procedure, and one on a command line carrying two
201	placeholders the page gave no way to fill. Every repair round had been adding words, and each new reader
202	met the seam where the newest words joined the old. Those instructions moved to the maintainer's page,
203	which defines the words they rest on.
204	
205	The thirteenth reading's eight blocking stops were then read as one set rather than eight repairs, and
206	seven of the eight were one class: the page used a word, a list, or a claim whose ground stood a hundred
207	lines further down, in another file, or in three senses at once. Six surface names arrived with their
208	definitions on the writer's page. The words seat, law, and tier were used from the top of the page and

426	
427	One class shows up across many sentences, so repairing the one sentence in front of a reader leaves
428	every other instance in place. The writer therefore records the class, and the steps below are how a
429	class becomes a rule.

431	1. A reader stops on a sentence. That reader is a cold reader or the owner, and both have opened rules.
432	   The writer writes the stop down in that reader's own words, including the guess the reader made

435	   the spec, or a habit picked up in chat. A class opens once the writer finds the same stop coming out

438	   an entry carries and is the list to write a new entry against. The status on a new entry says that

440	   catcher under the rule.
